title: She Mistranslated One Question to Protect Audrey Hepburn
title_alternatives: She Mistranslated One Question to Protect Audrey Hepburn
The Interpreter Broke the One Rule of Her Profession. Once.
For 29 Years She Sat Behind Audrey Hepburn and Said Nothing
Audrey Hepburn Heard the Real Question. She Answered the Fake One.
Her Job Was to Be Invisible. In 1981 She Stopped, for Two Seconds.
description:
The chair is always placed slightly behind and to the left. Behind, so the journalist looks at the subject and not at you. To the left, because most people turn right when they are thinking and you do not want to be in the way of that.

You do not lean forward. You do not react to anything that is said — not to a joke, not to bad news, not to a lie. If a question is rude, you translate it exactly as rude as it was. If the answer is evasive, you preserve the evasion precisely, including the pauses. You do not improve anything.

Giulia Sarti was taught this at twenty-two by a man who had done it at trade negotiations. He told her the job was not to be a bridge, because a bridge is a thing you see. The job was to be a window nobody notices is there, and the measure of a good day was that at the end of it neither party could describe your face.

She did it for twenty-nine years, in about two hundred sessions with the same actress. They were not friends. By her own count they had eleven conversations that were not work. She was offered money for what she knew on four occasions and turned it down every time — not out of loyalty, she said, because loyalty would have implied a relationship, and there was not one.

Then, in October 1981, in the eleventh minute of an interview, a young journalist asked a question that assumed something about the actress's father that was not true. And Giulia had somewhere between one and two seconds to decide what to do.

What she did was the only unprofessional act of her working life. The actress heard both versions, and said nothing, then or ever.

This story is a work of fiction. Giulia, the interview, the diaries and every detail in it are invented, created for storytelling and not drawn from any record.
